paragraphs: When people are no longer joined to one another by firm and lasting ties, you cannot win the cooperation of any great number of them unless you can persuade each person whose help you need that his own private interest obliges him to unite his efforts voluntarily with the efforts of all the rest. This can be done regularly and conveniently only through a newspaper. Nothing but a newspaper can drop the same thought into a thousand minds at the same moment. A newspaper is an adviser who does not have to be sought out. It comes of its own accord and talks with you briefly every day about the common good, without drawing you away from your private affairs.

Newspapers therefore become more necessary as people become more equal and individualism becomes more to be feared. To suppose that they serve only to protect freedom would be to underrate them: they sustain civilization. I do not deny that in democratic countries newspapers often lead citizens to launch ill-considered schemes together. But without newspapers there would be no common action at all. The harm they do is therefore much smaller than the harm they cure.

A newspaper does more than suggest the same purpose to a great number of people. It also supplies the means for carrying out together the plans that each of them may have conceived alone. In an aristocratic country, the leading citizens can see one another from far off, and when they want to join forces, they move toward each other and draw a crowd after them. In democratic countries, on the contrary, it often happens that a great number of people who wish or need to combine cannot do so. Each of them is very insignificant and lost in the crowd, so they cannot see one another and do not know where to find one another. A newspaper then takes up the idea or the feeling that had occurred to each of them at the same moment, but separately. All of them are immediately drawn toward this beacon, and these wandering minds, which had long searched for each other in the dark, meet at last and unite.

The newspaper brought them together, and the newspaper is still necessary to keep them united. For an association among a democratic people to have any power, it must be a numerous body. The people who make it up are therefore scattered over a wide area, and each of them is kept in his own home by the narrowness of his income or by the small, unceasing efforts with which he earns it. A way must then be found for them to talk every day without seeing one another, and to take common action without having met. Hardly any democratic association can do without newspapers. There is therefore a necessary connection between public associations and newspapers: newspapers make associations, and associations make newspapers. It has been correctly said that associations will grow in number as the conditions of men become more equal. It is no less certain that the number of newspapers grows in proportion to the number of associations. That is why in America we find at the same time the greatest number of associations and of newspapers.

This connection between the number of newspapers and the number of associations leads us to discover a further connection, between the state of the periodical press and the form of administration in a country. It shows that the number of newspapers must fall or rise among a democratic people according to how centralized or uncentralized its administration is. For among democratic nations, local powers cannot be entrusted to the leading members of the community, as they are in aristocracies. Those powers must either be abolished or placed in the hands of very large numbers of men. These men then form, in effect, an association permanently established by law to administer the affairs of a certain stretch of territory. They need a journal to bring them some news every day, in the midst of their own small concerns, about the state of their public affairs. The more numerous the local powers are, the greater the number of men in whom the law vests them. And since this need is felt every hour, the more abundantly newspapers multiply.

The extraordinary subdivision of administrative power has much more to do with the enormous number of American newspapers than the country’s great political freedom or the absolute liberty of its press. Suppose all the inhabitants of the Union had the vote, but a vote that extended only to choosing their legislators in Congress. They would need few newspapers, because they would have to act together only on a few very important but very rare occasions. But within the broad association of the nation, the law has established lesser associations in every county, every city, and indeed every village, for the purposes of local administration. The laws of the country thus compel every American to cooperate every day of his life with some of his fellow citizens for a common purpose, and each of them needs a newspaper to tell him what all the others are doing.

I am of the opinion that a democratic people *a without any national representative assemblies, but with a great number of small local powers, would in the end have more newspapers than another people governed by a centralized administration and an elected legislature. What best explains to me the enormous circulation of the daily press in the United States is that among the Americans I find the greatest national freedom combined with local freedom of every kind. There is a prevailing opinion in France and England that the circulation of newspapers would increase indefinitely if the taxes laid on the press were removed. This greatly exaggerates the effects of such a reform. Newspapers increase in number not according to how cheap they are, but according to how often a great number of people feel the need to communicate and combine.

[Footnote a: I say a democratic people. The administration of an aristocratic people may be the reverse of centralized, and yet the need for newspapers may be little felt, because local powers are then placed in the hands of a very small number of men. These men either act separately, or they know each other and can easily meet and come to an understanding.]

In the same way, I would attribute the growing influence of the daily press to causes more general than those usually given. A newspaper can survive only on the condition that it publishes feelings or principles shared by a large number of people. A newspaper therefore always represents an association made up of its regular readers. This association may be more or less defined, more or less restricted, more or less numerous. But the very fact that the newspaper stays alive proves that at least the seed of such an association exists in the minds of its readers.

This leads me to one last reflection, with which I shall end this chapter. The more equal the conditions of men become, and the weaker men are as individuals, the more easily they give way to the current of the multitude, and the harder it is for them to hold on alone to an opinion the multitude has abandoned. A newspaper represents an association. It may be said to speak to each of its readers in the name of all the others, and to influence them in proportion to their individual weakness. The power of the newspaper press must therefore increase as the social conditions of men become more equal.
